articles.title: Twenty-Five Years After 9/11, Lower Manhattan Is Both a Tribute and a Promise
articles.fullContent:
By Rob Reilly ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ brings the people shaping advertising, commerce, and media together for four days of unscripted conversations and after-hours connections. Meet us in Midtown, Oct. 5–8.

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, I stood on Hudson Street watching in shock as WTC 1 fell.

In the days and years that followed, the future of New York City’s Financial District seemed bleak. Nobody would want to go back there, the thinking went. The wound was too deep.

There was an open scar in the middle of the city, a 16-acre void we called “the pit,” spanned by temporary pedestrian bridges. For a long time, it felt like nothing could rise from it.

But then, the steel started to climb. One World Trade finally broke street level and inched toward the skyline. Over the course of a decade, New York City did what it does best: move forward without forgetting.

In 2013, WPP took a chance. Our global media collective GroupM—now called WPP Media—signed one of the first long-term leases at 3 World Trade Center, at the time the largest new office commitment in a World Trade Center building. It was an investment in a vision that Larry Silverstein, who led redevelopment of the site, and Mayor Michael Bloomberg were determined to see come to fruition.

Other corporations including Condé Nast, Spotify, and Fast Company also came to plant their flags downtown.

With them came restaurants, young residents, culture—an organic gravitational pull. Lower Manhattan’s population has doubled since 2000, according to the New York State Comptroller, and the Financial District saw the biggest rise in apartment searches of any neighborhood across the five boroughs in 2025 on StreetEasy.

I often think about what it means to work at the World Trade Center.

I pass the memorial pools on my way to the office every morning, where families and tourists stand in reflection. The Oculus is visible from my office window, and to enter it is to stand inside the ribs of something ancient and alive—a daily reminder of where I am.

In our industry, it’s easy to get caught up in the stress of the job. But then the weight of what happened here hits, a reminder to not take a single day for granted.

I also think of this place as the embodiment of resilience, powered by creativity.

Architects, developers, and city planners had to rebuild Lower Manhattan to honor the lives lost, while empowering a community to feel hopeful about the future. Creativity is the ultimate act of optimism. Imagination, collaboration, design, are gestures toward tomorrow.

Lower Manhattan is a living, breathing tribute where people work, create, and live every single day. A place forever anchored by remembrance, yet surrounded by hope.

Rob Reilly is the global chief creative officer of WPP.

articles.title: Former CNN Photographer Recalls What It Was Like to Record the Newsroom on 9/11
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro At 8:49 a.m. ET, on September 11, 2001, CNN abruptly returned from a commercial break showing a live video image of smoke billowing out of a gaping hole in one of the twin towers at the World Trade Center.

Carol Lin , a CNN anchor at that time, relayed to viewers the little she knew of the unfolding situation, saying they had unconfirmed reports of a plane crashing into one of the towers, adding, “CNN Center right now is just beginning to work on this story, obviously calling our sources and trying to figure out exactly what happened.”

Atlanta-based CNN videographer Ric Blackburn was on bump-shot duty that Tuesday morning, capturing shots of the CNN newsroom inside its former home at the CNN Center going into and out of commercial breaks for the network’s morning news shows.

Upon seeing the rising newsroom chaos following the first plane crash, Blackburn’s journalism instincts immediately kicked in, and he started documenting what he saw.

The CNN original’s incredible recording is available in two parts on YouTube and offers a rare vantage point on how a global operation like CNN responded to one of the biggest stories of the century. This internal account of what happened inside the CNN building amazingly captures how the network’s journalists responded and adjusted to the growing calamity in real time.

Speaking exclusively to TVNewser, Blackburn, who is now retired, recalls his experience that Tuesday morning. He said that, for the 16 video journalists stationed in Atlanta, to give them a break from all the traveling they did, they’d go on a one-month rotation at a time inside the CNN Center doing bump-shot duty.

It was his turn that month, and his shift began at 5 a.m. and was to run until 2 p.m. ET. As the intensity of the newsroom picked up, he called his supervisor and requested his regular camera and a boom microphone to capture the sound.

Blackburn’s recording starts around 9:25 a.m. ET, and by that time the second plane had already crashed into the second tower, with the gravity of the situation well established.

“I just started roaming the newsroom, people on the phone, people looking up at the monitors, people talking to each other, and it just crescendoed, like a loud crescendo as time went on,” Blackburn said.

He noted that Walter Isaacson , CNN’s president at that time, was not initially thrilled with his work capturing the newsroom and the many conversations happening in real time.

“He told me several times to ‘get the F out of the newsroom with that camera.’ I just kind of ignored him because he seemed too serious. Because I knew what I was doing,” Blackburn said.

Other CNN executives shown in the footage, besides Isaacson, include Sid Bedingfield , Tom Johnson , Jim Walton , Earl Casey , Jamie Kellner , Eason Jordan , Sue Bunda , and Jane Maxwell .

CNN founder, the late Ted Turner , also makes an appearance in the video, with Blackburn recalling that they knew it was a huge story when Turner initially walked into the newsroom shortly after the first plane hit the tower, “with his hands clasped over his face, just looking up at the monitors, and kind of shaking his head.”

At one point, Blackburn captures Turner, Isaacson, and Jordan discussing whether the other Turner news and entertainment networks should switch to CNN’s coverage, with Jordan later on informing Turner that the first tower had collapsed. A shocked Turner wonders who could have orchestrated such an attack, speculating it was the Taliban.

Blackburn seemed to have some fortuitous luck that morning, capturing key moments related to CNN and its programming decisions, including the discussion of introducing Aaron Brown to CNN’s airwaves; appearances of various CNN on-air talent at that time, including Daryn Kagan , Leon Harris , Bill Hemmer , and Lou Waters ; technical issues concerning bringing the network’s signal down from New York City; the CNN Center being closed down and restricted to essential staff only; and food and beverage being transported to the newsrooms.

Interestingly, his camera was also present when a brief verbal fight broke out inside CNN’s control room.

Blackburn was also present as staffers received and reacted to announcements about the ongoing tragedy. This also included initial reports of fire at the Pentagon; the White House being evacuated; the airports closed and all planes being grounded; the collapse of the first tower; and news of a plane down in Somerset, Pennsylvania.

As he went on chronicling what was happening inside the building, he noted a work mode shift, transitioning from a sense of chaos to an acceptance of their new reality, saying, “I believe that that’s what’s amazing about CNN is they knew what’s ahead of them.”

Blackburn said he worked until 12:30 p.m. ET, when he received word of his next assignment, traveling 18 hours by van to New York City, where he would be stationed for the next month and a half.

While up there, he said, “there was such a solemn, disbelief, surreal feeling in the whole city,” compounded by the smell of burning bodies and hair in the air: “It was like a twilight zone,” he added.

The 34-year CNN veteran wasn’t fond of his time in the city, saying there was a sad, expressionless feeling, with people coming to his camera with pictures of loved ones.

However, he considers himself lucky, from a journalistic point of view. His footage will forever remain a window into how newsrooms operated before today’s new tech, all the while covering “one of the craziest things” in his life.

Ticker: Technical Issues Temporarily Forced CNN Off the Air Mark Mwachiro

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Dashboard That Makes Your Case for You
articles.fullContent:
By Ryan Joe The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

One of the biggest goals of ADWEEK’s Brandweek conference next week is to give participants practical skills that will help them grow in their careers.

So ADWEEK and Code and Theory are partnering once again to offer a beginner-intermediate level masterclass on how to use AI to build a live dashboard that you and your team will actually use.

Code and Theory’s Karen Piper , head of strategy, and Pete Steiner, head of Creative Labs, will teach you how to build the dashboard, power it with the right datasets, shape the data, and automate it so it’s continuously giving you the most important information when you need it.

After all, the brick of Excel sheets that Gary from IT started in 1991 just doesn’t cut it in 2026.

“Marketers will get reports or produce reports that have half the information, and they don’t have everything they need to make decisions on the next step, or to report on themes and trends effectively,” said Piper.

Off-the-shelf solutions might be convenient, but they don’t always have the configurations marketers need. Those who build their own, however, can make it their own.

Piper builds dashboards for every pitch. Doing so allows her to share the data in one place across different teams involved in the pitch. It also helps her consolidate data such as case studies on different programs like PowerPoint and Keynote that exist in different places across the holding company.

Steiner has a dashboard to run his teams, all of whom are working on three or four different projects at various stages of maturity. “It helps me understand what state every project is in, who’s assigned to it, and what resources are attached to it,” he said. It also lets his leadership have a quick view into all the work happening across the Creative Labs team.

AI makes building a dashboard accessible, which is both a blessing and a curse. It’s easy to build all sorts of bells and whistles, and even easier to let them get out of hand.

This class will teach participants a necessary skill: properly scoping out your project.

“You need a really clear outline, almost like a product requirement document,” said Piper. “How many people are going to use this? Do they need logins? Do we need to keep this updated over the long term? How is data coming in? Thinking about all of that before you start will help you stay focused.”

The class will go beyond vibe coding a dashboard—it’ll teach you how to properly plan and build an endurable product that you and your team use for a long time.

Register for Brandweek if you haven’t already. The class takes place Wednesday, Sept. 18 at the Spotlight Stage North from 1-1:45 p.m.

Space is limited, so entry will be granted on a first-come basis.

Ryan Joe is the editor in chief of Adweek.

What do agency leaders need right now? According to Ross Martin, maybe “a sanity check and a lobotomy.”

In this special episode of Marketing Vanguard, host Jenny Rooney spotlights the launch of ADWEEK’s Agencies Vanguard program with three founding members: Jessica Henrichs, CEO of DonerColle Partners; Ross Martin, president of Known; and Chioma Aduba, president of Droga5.

Together, they unpack why agency leadership has become one of the most complex jobs in business, why competitors need spaces for radical honesty, and why the future of agencies cannot be solved in isolation.

How leaders can build organizations that adapt through change

Why agency executives need safe spaces for honest conversation

What diverse agency models can learn from one another

Jessica Henrichs is the CEO of DonerColle Partners and one of the founding members of Adweek’s Agencies Vanguard program. In this episode, she brings a clear perspective on adaptive leadership, the value of peer support and why agency leaders need to build belief through change rather than pretend they have every answer.

Ross Martin is the president of Known and a founding member of Agencies Vanguard. Known for his candid take on the agency industry, Ross brings a sharp view on the structural challenges facing agencies today, from outdated business models to the bigger question of what the industry wants to stand for next.

Chioma Aduba is the president of Droga5 and a founding member of Agencies Vanguard. In this conversation, she speaks to the value of transparency, cross-agency community and creating an industry that feels like it is in good hands for the next generation of creative talent.

[03:10] Why Leaders Need Perspective, Not Certainty — Jessica Henrichs opens with a line that cuts through the usual leadership cosplay: leaders do not need to pretend they have every answer. What they do need is perspective. For agency leaders, the job now is to build organizations that can adapt, give people confidence through change and create belief in where the business is headed. That kind of leadership requires fearlessness, not because leaders are never unsure, but because they have to keep moving people through discomfort anyway.

[04:03] Agency Leaders Need a Sanity Check — Ross Martin answers the question of what agency leaders need now with the kind of honesty that makes people laugh because it feels a little too true: “a sanity check and a lobotomy.” His point is that running an agency in 2026 means taking on some of the hardest challenges in business. The value is not only access to thought leadership or the clout of Adweek. It is the possibility of brokering more provocative conversations, learning from different perspectives and letting the concentration of big bets embolden leaders to make more change.

[25:13] What Should Agencies Be Known For? — Ross closes with the episode’s sharpest industry-wide challenge: what do agencies want to be known for? Opaque business models, perverse incentives and cultures that fail too many people? Or systems of innovation where art, science and technology come together, clients can trust and grow, and people are proud to work? That is the question Agencies Vanguard is designed to help leaders wrestle with. Not politely. Seriously.

articles.title: Will social media bans reshape the future of marketing?
articles.fullContent:
Conditions online can be harrowing. All of us are susceptible to doom-scrolling—absorbing the intensity of global political, humanitarian and climate crises with the flick of a thumb. Not to mention comparing our lives to influencers’ glossy content or our acquaintances’ highlight reels, letting unhealthy comparisons rear their ugly head.

With such dark sides to social, lawmakers worldwide have started to wonder: Do they have a responsibility to enact social media bans that protect children? Consumers think so, with 68% saying they support such bans, according to Sprout Social’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey. Those with young children are the most likely to rally behind them.

For social media marketers, who already face a number of internal and external challenges in the course of doing their jobs, this means even more stress and brand safety risks. Many countries have already implemented, passed or strongly considered a social media ban. And Meta’s landmark youth safety settlement means a new series of safeguards will be required on Instagram and Facebook, with a call for more networks to follow suit.

This new legislation may make it more difficult to reach certain audiences, publish content efficiently, and stay compliant with ever-changing rule books and country-specific laws. Zooming out, as the world’s economies become more connected, it’s going to prove challenging for global brands to comply with so many disparate policies and maintain relevance.

To make it easier to navigate, we’ve laid out the facts we have so far about current and proposed social media bans. We’ve also asked global marketers for their takes on how social teams should adjust their workflows and content strategies as regulations around social media become more common.

Please note the information provided in this article does not, and is not intended to, constitute formal legal advice. Please review our full disclaimer before reading any further.

Networks are regulating in response to public concern and settlements

Social media networks are responding to proposed legislation and judicial decisions by updating their functionality and adding safeguards, like parental controls, for youth safety.

Per the Q1 2026 Sprout Pulse Survey, consumers were more likely to support networks implementing parental consent measures and age verification technology over outright bans. In lockstep with consumer preferences, many major platforms now give parents more control over their children’s experience online.

Networks like Meta, Snapchat, WhatsApp and YouTube are tightening parental controls, designing family-friendly app experiences, enforcing time limits and restricting sensitive content to improve the social media experience for younger generations. They’re also giving parents a broader window into what kids are doing online–offering ways to manage child privacy settings, supervise activity and limit conversations with AI chatbots.

The overarching impact of the Meta youth safety settlement

While networks have slowly started to self-regulate, the latest Meta youth safety settlement has fast tracked several changes to pay attention to.

Through the terms of the settlement, Meta has agreed to enforce the following restrictions to make their platforms safer for kids:

  • Two-hour daily time limit
  • Turning off nighttime access to their apps
  • No notifications during school hours to limit interruptions during critical learning periods
  • Prompts that interrupt teens after 15 minutes of continuous screen time to lessen mindless scrolling
  • More parental controls to empower parents to design the experience they want for their children

These terms cement changes that will likely extend beyond Instagram and Facebook, too, with part of Meta’s payout depending on TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat adopting similar rules.

It’s also worth noting, this settlement sets a precedent: constraints on reaching minors are arriving faster through settlements than through official legislation.

How brands can adjust to social media restrictions

Even if you aren’t operating within the jurisdiction of a legislative social media ban, the incoming changes based on the Meta settlement begs the question: what does this mean for brands?

Know what to expect

First and foremost, it’s critical to understand how these changes will impact your brand (if at all). Changes to your brand’s strategy and overall marketing tactics should be minimal since these new safeguards benefit youth demographics that brands don’t market to.

But, there are a few downstream impacts to understand:

  • Creator audiences could deflate: Experts predict stricter age restrictions will expose creator audiences inflated by youth demographics that aren’t a fit for your brand. It’ll be even more critical to audit creator demographics to ensure audiences aren’t younger than advertised, making it the right time to shift to a partnership model based on topical alignment rather than demographics alone.
  • Vanity metrics will decline: Capped usage, hidden likes and non-personalized feeds mean marketers could see a decline in vanity metrics (think: likes and impressions). This is a net-positive for all involved—a safer experience for youth and less of a focus on metrics that don’t have material impact on your brand. Instead, shift focus to look at stronger engagement and conversion metrics to understand what’s happening with the people who actually have buying power.

Prioritize age-aligned content

While the days of trying to reach everyone on social are long behind us, teams can’t only rely on the algorithms to deliver their content to the right people. Legislation headwinds will require brands to be more audience-specific when crafting their content.

Sam Morgan-Smith, Head of Social at the UK-based PR agency The Romans, describes this shift: “The days of blanket posting (or ‘throwing confetti’ as I refer to it) and trusting the algorithm are over. Brands will need to get far more strategic. Content needs to be age-aware and legally defensible.”

articles.title: YouTube Gives You Feedback On Shorts Before Publishing via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
YouTube is expanding a tool that reviews Shorts before they’re published. Get Feedback is currently expanding to all creators in the U.S. who are over 18 and using the main YouTube app on Android or iPhone, YouTube said in a Creator Insider video published September 9.

You’ll see the tool as a button on the Add Details screen during the regular Shorts upload process. YouTube’s Help documentation says tapping it provides an analysis of your video’s hook, pacing, and more, and offers suggestions for improvements but doesn’t make changes itself.

In the Creator Insider video, Rene Ritchie, YouTube’s creator liaison, says the tool’s guidance covers the strength of your hook, pacing, and visuals. He points out an example praising a news update’s delivery and audio quality, with suggestions to add cutaway visuals or screen recordings. The video doesn’t cover all the checks the tool performs.

Creators can revisit and refine their Shorts before publishing. Ritchie said “getting and using this feedback is entirely optional.” The tool doesn’t edit anything on its own. As Ritchie put it, “it just provides suggestions based on best practices, and YouTube knows every creator, channel, and audience is different.”

Get Feedback appeared earlier than September 9. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan shared the news about the tool on X on August 24. In his post, he mentioned that it was in the process of rolling out and told creators to “upload an unlisted draft to get tailored suggestions on a video’s hooks, pacing, and structure.” The September 9 video and the Help page describe a button inside the upload flow instead, and neither mentions unlisted drafts.

YouTube has been exploring a closely related experiment called VibeCheck through YouTube Labs , which is open to people in the U.S. The Labs page describes VibeCheck as an AI coach that helps analyze a Short’s pacing, hooks, and lighting, accessible via a Try VibeCheck button on the Add Details page. The sources reviewed don’t explain whether VibeCheck and Get Feedback are linked, and neither the Creator Insider video nor the Help page describes Get Feedback as AI-powered.

YouTube’s audience-performance data becomes available after your video is published, while Get Feedback provides guidance earlier in the process. Nothing in the announcement claims these suggestions predict views or improve results. The tool’s feedback doesn’t replace the retention and engagement data you already track.

YouTube says Get Feedback is currently expanding, so not every eligible creator may see the button yet. The video doesn’t mention other countries, desktop, or YouTube Studio.

The sources reviewed don’t explain how the suggestions are generated.

articles.title: The brand loyalty playbook: What it really is and how to build it
articles.fullContent:
Brand loyalty has always been hard to win. Today, it’s even easier to lose.

Consumers increasingly encounter brands across social networks, creator communities and other digital spaces businesses don’t control. At the same time, the rise of AI-generated content and misinformation has made people more skeptical about what they see online.

Customer sentiment can shift quickly in this environment, so brands need to understand what people are saying while those conversations still matter. Sales data, surveys and quarterly reports reveal useful patterns, but by the time teams use them, customers may already feel differently, or their loyalty is too far gone.

Building lasting brand loyalty depends on how quickly brands understand what audiences are saying, what’s driving those conversations and how to respond. Social intelligence gives teams a real-time view of what customers care about and how expectations are shifting.

In this guide, we’ll explore what brand loyalty really means, why it’s harder to earn and how brands can strengthen it.

What is brand loyalty? (And how it’s different from brand affinity)

What is brand loyalty?

Brand loyalty is a customer’s ongoing preference for one brand over its competitors, driven by trust and emotional connection rather than convenience or habit alone.

Brand loyalty is evident in what customers do: repeatedly choosing the same brand, recommending it to others or sticking with it when competitors offer a cheaper or more convenient option.

Brand affinity reflects what customers feel: a sense of connection to a brand based on shared values, identity or experiences.

The two often reinforce each other, but they aren’t interchangeable. The same goes for customer loyalty and brand awareness.

What it measures Example signal Brand loyalty A customer’s ongoing preference for a brand Repeatedly choosing the brand over competitors Brand affinity Engagement and emotional connection to a brand Feeling that the brand reflects your values or identity Customer loyalty Repeat behavior based on the overall customer relationship Continuing to buy because of service, rewards or convenience Brand awareness Familiarity with or recognition of a brand Recognizing the brand name, logo or products

Think of brand loyalty like a lasting friendship. One good conversation rarely creates a close relationship. Trust builds through repeated experiences that show someone is reliable and understands what matters to you.

Brands earn loyalty in much the same way. Each positive interaction gives customers another reason to return, while repeated missteps chip away at loyalty over time.

Why brand loyalty is harder to earn

Brand loyalty now competes with a much wider range of influences. A customer might discover a product through a creator, read mixed reviews on Reddit and see a critical TikTok about the company before they ever visit the brand’s website. By then, they’ve already formed an impression.

People are also approaching online content with more skepticism. According to Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey, 35% of social users say their trust in social content has decreased over the past year. Misinformation was the most common reason, cited by 30% of respondents. Another 20% pointed to unregulated AI content. And 88% agree AI video tools have reduced their trust in the news they see on social.

Brand interactions face the same scrutiny. An overly polished testimonial might feel less credible if customers suspect AI involvement. A vague response to criticism can fuel more questions. A creator partnership can also backfire if the recommendation feels inauthentic or the sponsorship isn’t transparent.

The trust bar is higher now. Customers are paying closer attention to whether a company’s actions match what it says. Loyalty increasingly depends on the credibility brands build through every interaction, including those outside their own channels.

Why is brand loyalty important?

Brand loyalty gives businesses more stability in a crowded market. Loyal customers are more likely to keep choosing a brand even when competitors enter the picture, supporting several business outcomes:

  • Protect revenue: Loyal customers are less likely to churn. For example, a software company with strong loyalty may retain more subscribers after a competitor launches a lower-priced plan.
  • Lower acquisition pressure: A strong base of repeat customers reduces the need to replace every lost customer through paid acquisition.
  • Drive organic growth: Loyal customers often recommend brands through reviews, referrals and social conversation. A recommendation in a niche community can influence new buyers without the brand having to initiate it.
  • Strengthen business planning: Consistent loyalty can make revenue more predictable and reveal what customers value. Repeated praise for a specific feature, for instance, gives product teams clearer direction on where to invest.

Taken together, loyalty becomes a brand health marker, not just a marketing KPI.

How brands miss the loyalty signal

Most brands aren’t short on customer data. The problem is often timing.

A complaint might surface on social days before it comes up in a customer survey. Customers might start expecting a feature your competitor just launched before sales data reflects the shift. By the time the right team gets the information, the best window to respond may have passed.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that 86% of professionals say they’ve missed opportunities in the past two years because consumer insights were delayed, siloed or underused. Reacting too slowly to a market shift was the most common missed opportunity, cited by 33% of respondents. And only 10% of organizations say they can act on a social insight within hours.

How teams capture and organize customer data contributes to the gap. Different systems capture different parts of the customer picture:

  • Business intelligence (BI) looks backward at business performance, including sales and revenue.
  • Customer intelligence (CI) captures current and past customer profiles and purchase history, often through CRM and transaction data.
  • Social intelligence adds human context by revealing what people are saying and how they feel right now.

Disconnected data makes it harder for teams to respond at the right moment. According to Sprout’s Q4 2025 Pulse Survey, 55% of consumers say brands do a good job listening but don’t always act on what they hear. Only 31% say brands do both well.

For loyalty, listening alone isn’t enough. Connecting real-time audience signals with other customer data gives teams the full picture and a chance to address problems before frustration turns into churn.

How to build brand loyalty that lasts

Social teams have the most influence on loyalty when what they learn from customers leads to better experiences. Here are six areas to focus on.

Key Takeaways

  • The global education sector is expected to reach $10 trillion in value by 2030, making digital marketing essential for standing out in this competitive industry.
  • Digital marketing in higher education means reaching four distinct audiences (students, parents, counselors, and B2B tech buyers) with messaging tailored to what they actually care about.

  • Proven strategies like local SEO, paid advertising, and social media engagement can drive enrollment and engagement.
  • The right tools, data-driven insights, and experienced agency support drive sustainable growth and measurable return on investment (ROI).

The global education sector is set to reach $10 trillion in value by 2030, powered by growth in developing markets as well as education technology reaching new heights. Both of those factors add up to a lot of competition out there for your education business or clients.

Compounding that is the fact that the way students and parents search for schools has changed. With a growing online audience and competition from all angles, institutions need to stand out, and digital marketing is how they’ll do it.

In this guide, we’re diving deep into the strategies that work, the challenges and common mistakes you might face, and how to conquer them like a pro. 

What Is Education Marketing?

Digital marketing for education encompasses the strategies and tools used by schools, universities, edtech companies, training centers, and any other business in the niche to promote their offerings online. It’s a multifaceted approach that includes:

  • Search engine optimization (SEO) for visibility: Building a well-optimized site puts your institution at the top of search results for relevant queries. 
  • Pay-per-click (PPC) campaigns: Buying PPC campaigns enables you to focus on more targeted traffic on conventional search engines like Google and Bing, social media, connected TV devices, or even in apps.
  • Social media engagement: Building meaningful connections with audiences on popular social media platforms gives you a chance to both improve your perception and draw in potential leads.
  • Content marketing: Creating value-driven content, such as blogs and videos, that address your audience’s pain points.

Why Digital Marketing Matters for Education

The education sector’s target audience (students, parents, and professionals) turns to the web to research options before making decisions. One study showed that when looking into higher education opportunities, 63 percent of students start their research on traditional search engines, and 60 percent used popular social media platforms. 

This applies across education, though. A school district shopping for software and new parents shopping for a daycare will both start online.

Digital marketing simplifies this process by delivering the right information at the right time. Educational institutions that invest in digital marketing can:

  • Build brand authority: A consistent online reputation helps establish your business as a trustworthy and reliable option. 
  • Enhance engagement: Digital marketing campaigns help your team connect with audiences where they are through meaningful and interactive content.
  • Boost conversions: Data-driven campaigns showing the value of your offerings will help convert inquiries into enrollments.

An effective digital campaign ensures that your business stays top of mind with your target audience, showing what you do best and moving them to a conversion.

What Makes Education Marketing Different

Marketing in the education sector presents unique challenges and opportunities. Here’s what sets it apart:

  1. Building Trust: Prospective students and parents alike are going to be concerned about the quality and credibility of institutions. The same applies to education technology (edtech) or other branches of the industry. Trust-building will be essential given the substantial investments in education.
  2. Long Decision Cycles: Customer decisions often involve months of research and multiple touchpoints. You need to build campaigns that can retain value during the entire cycle.
  3. Localized Marketing: An education marketing strategy tailored to the community where a specific school or business operates will perform much better than a broad, one-size-fits-all approach.
  4. Storytelling: A student’s educational experience is often an emotional journey for them, as well as their parents and teachers. Painting the picture of the role your school or business plays in that journey is critical for business conversions.
  5. Complex Stakeholders: Education marketing has to cater to students, parents, sponsors, and counselors simultaneously. Building out segments and personalized campaigns for each group is key to success.

Education Marketing Channels

No single channel carries an entire education marketing program on its own. The schools and edtech brands seeing the strongest results run a mix, meeting different audiences at different points in a decision cycle that can stretch on for months.

Below, I’ve broken down the four channels that consistently drive results in marketing for education. Each plays a specific role, and the smartest programs coordinate them to account for each customer’s unique buyer journey.

SEO and Local Search

Local SEO matters more in education than in most industries because most students and parents are searching for schools or programs nearby. That means researching location-based keywords and showing up in local search results is disproportionately important to your education marketing strategy compared to other channels.

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Brand safety is the practice of protecting a brand’s reputation by controlling where and how it appears online, from ad placements to social media publishing.

What is brand safety?

Brand safety is the set of practices that keep a brand’s ads, content, and conversations away from harmful, offensive, or misleading environments. It applies to paid media, where an ad might appear next to violent or extremist content, and to organic social, where a poorly reviewed post or an unmoderated comment thread can create the same reputational damage.

Most enterprise teams anchor their approach to industry standards. The Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), a voluntary cross-industry initiative created in 2019 that the World Federation of Advertisers discontinued on August 9, 2024, produced the Brand Safety Floor, which defined the content categories advertisers universally avoid, such as hate speech, explicit content, and terrorism.

Although the initiative itself no longer operates, its Brand Safety Floor and Adjacency Standards Framework remain widely used as legacy industry reference points. The IAB and accredited verification vendors then measure whether placements actually stayed inside those lines.

The practical point for marketers: Brand safety is not a single tool or a one-time audit. It is a system of standards, workflows, and monitoring that has to work across every team touching your brand. For a broader look at the fundamentals, see our guide to protecting your brand across social channels.

Brand safety vs. brand suitability

Brand safety is about avoiding content that no advertiser wants to be near, while brand suitability is about deciding what’s appropriate for your specific brand, audience, and moment. Safety is the universal floor. Suitability is where your own values, category, and risk tolerance come in.

A news article about a natural disaster clears the brand safety floor. It may still be unsuitable for a travel brand running a beach campaign. Both decisions matter, but they’re made by different people using different criteria.

In short: Safety keeps you out of trouble, suitability keeps you on-brand.

The risk landscape has shifted as AI-generated content, automated amplification, and creator-led media have all scaled at once. Most incidents enterprise teams face today fall into one of five categories.

  • Ad placement next to harmful or inappropriate content
  • Bots, trolls, and coordinated inauthentic behavior
  • Unvetted influencer partnerships
  • Misinformation and AI-generated deepfakes

Programmatic buying accounts for over 90% of US digital display ad spending, which means adjacency decisions happen faster than any human can review them. A single misconfigured campaign can put your logo next to content that contradicts everything your brand stands for.

Inclusion lists (approved placements only) give tighter control than exclusion lists, which chase problems after they appear. Most enterprise teams run both, paired with keyword and category blocks, and audit placement reports monthly rather than at campaign wrap.

Bots, trolls, and coordinated inauthentic behavior

Automated accounts can flood a comment section, distort sentiment data, and make a minor complaint look like a mass backlash. Coordinated groups do the same thing deliberately, often targeting brands during product launches or public announcements.

The danger is not just the noise. It’s that teams overreact to manufactured outrage or miss a genuine issue buried underneath it. Reliable listening data and a clear threshold for what counts as a real incident help teams tell the difference.

Unvetted influencer partnerships

When a creator’s past content or ongoing behavior surfaces mid-campaign, the association lands on your brand. Vetting has to cover more than follower counts: past posts, audience authenticity, brand conflicts, and how the creator handles criticism.

What is a social intelligence tool?

A social intelligence tool helps brands turn online conversations into insights about their audience, market, and broader culture.

These tools mostly deal with unprompted data. People aren’t filling out a survey. They’re venting, joking, sharing recommendations in forums, and filming reviews for YouTube and TikTok.

Social intelligence vs. social listening vs. social media analytics

All three run on social data, but they answer different questions:

  • Social media analytics is about performance: How is our social content performing?
  • Social listening is about conversation: What are people saying about our brand, competitors, or industry?
  • Social intelligence pushes more into interpretation: What do those conversations actually tell us about our audience, our market, and what we should do next?

Here’s a quick breakdown of the biggest differences:

So, when should you take the leap to social intelligence?

Dylan Peterkin, a social intelligence expert, says teams tend to outgrow basic listening tools when their goals “move past performance and shift into understanding audiences and culture.”

A basic tool can help you measure what you spent on an idea and how it performed with your existing audience, but there’s no replacement for full-fledged intelligence: being where your target audience is, and finding ways to exist in those spaces naturally through product AND content.

In short, once your questions get bigger than campaign performance, basic listening starts to feel pretty limited.

What should you look for in a social intelligence tool?

Look for broad data coverage, real noise reduction, trend and theme detection, and AI-powered analysis, all wrapped in an interface your whole team can actually understand. 

Let’s take a closer look at what to look out for:

Data coverage

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media archiving captures posts, comments, edits, deletions, and metadata in a legally defensible format for regulatory compliance.
  2. Government, finance, healthcare, and education sectors face distinct archiving mandates under FOIA, SEC/FINRA, HIPAA, and FERPA.
  3. Compliant workflows require automated real-time capture, metadata preservation, searchable storage, and regular audits.
  4. Enterprise platforms like Hootsuite Social OS integrate with archiving solutions to automate compliance across teams and accounts.

What is social media archiving?

Social media archiving is the process of capturing, preserving, and storing all social media content in a secure, legally defensible format. That includes posts, comments, direct messages, multimedia, edits, deletions, and the metadata behind all of it.

Social media posted by government agencies is generally treated as a public record under FOIA and state open records laws, and in finance and healthcare, social messages count as regulated business communications.

For government agencies, social media is a public forum and must be archived as part of open records laws. Financial institutions, healthcare providers, and educational institutions face their own archiving mandates under regulations like SEC/FINRA rules, HIPAA, and FERPA.

A proper archive of your social media content and communication allows you to respond to eDiscovery, public records, and Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. You also need archived social comments if you are faced with a First Amendment challenge.

Your content is publicly available on your social accounts, but that’s not enough. Social media platforms are private-sector companies. They are not subject to open records laws, and there’s no guarantee they will preserve your content indefinitely.

Platform API changes can also restrict access to historical data without warning. A purpose-built archiving solution is the only way to maintain a complete, tamper-proof record.

Bonus: Download a free bundle of social media tools designed specifically for government — including post ideas and templates for social media policies, strategies, reports, and crisis communications.

Why is social media archiving important for regulated industries?

Social media archiving is a foundational risk management strategy that protects regulated organizations from legal exposure while building public trust. Without a systematic archiving process, agencies and institutions risk being unable to respond to records requests, audits, or litigation.

  • Legal compliance: Federal, state, and industry-specific regulations require organizations to retain social media records for defined periods. Archiving ensures you meet those obligations.
  • Audit readiness: Regulators can request records at any time. A searchable, well-organized archive means your team can respond quickly and completely.
  • eDiscovery preparedness: In legal proceedings, social media content is increasingly subject to discovery requests. Archived records with metadata provide the documentation courts require.
  • Risk mitigation: Archiving protects your organization from penalties, fines, and lawsuits that result from incomplete or missing records.
  • Transparency and public trust: For government agencies especially, accessible archives demonstrate accountability to constituents and the media.
  • Operational efficiency: Centralized, searchable archives reduce the time and effort required to locate specific content across multiple accounts and platforms.

Social media compliance starts with having the records to prove it.

How is social media archiving regulated across industries?

Regulations differ by state, country, and industry, but the core obligation is the same: preserve everything. Social media content is generally treated as part of the public record or as a business communication, subject to specific retention and privacy requirements.

Regulated organizations need to maintain an archive of social media content, including posts, comments, direct messages, and conversations. These records must be accessible for audits, public information requests, and legal discovery.

While the specific requirements differ by sector, most regulations require the following:

  • Metadata collection: Capturing timestamps, user information, and device details for every post and comment.
  • Original format retention: Preserving content exactly as it appeared when published, including edits and deletions.
  • Retention period: Storing records for a legally defined period, which varies by jurisdiction and industry.
  • Comment archiving: Retaining comments, even if they are edited, deleted, or hidden.
  • Contextual recordkeeping: Maintaining entire conversation threads, not just isolated comments.
  • Data location: Storing data in specific geographic regions to comply with privacy laws.

articles.title: Real Estate Marketing: A Complete Guide for 2026
articles.fullContent:
If you’re running marketing for a real estate brand, you already know the deal. Zillow, Realtor.com, and Redfin sit at the top of nearly every high-volume query, and AI Overviews are quietly compressing what’s left of the informational clicks below. That’s the real estate marketing challenge in 2026. Everyone else has already adopted the basics, so pulling ahead now takes a creative, targeted strategy.

This guide walks through a five-step framework for building a real estate marketing plan. From there, you’ll get a breakdown of how AI search and portal competition are reshaping the search engine results pages (SERPs), plus a client case study showing what real growth looks like when the strategy lands.

You’ll finish this guide with a clear picture of what to do next for your real estate marketing strategy in 2026.

Key Takeaways

  • Zillow, Realtor.com, and Redfin dominate head-term SERPs, so marketing wins come from targeting long-tail and hyperlocal queries the portals ignore. 
  • Google’s AI Overviews are causing people to click less. Structure content for AI citation and reinforce E-E-A-T signals to stay visible. 
  • A five-step marketing plan (ICPs, brand identity, website, omnichannel, offline) is the foundation. Skip a step and everything downstream weakens. 
  • Owned channels like email and direct mail are how “the little guy” can fight against the real estate giants by routing buyers around third-party portals. 
  • NP Digital used the tactics in this guide to stack significant wins for our client, Homeway Real Estate.

What Is Real Estate Marketing?

Real estate marketing is the practice of promoting properties available for sale or rent. It takes the Four Ps of marketing (Product, Price, Place, and Promotion) and adapts them to the real estate market. 

The marketing plan is important because of the hyper-competitive nature of the real estate industry. A proper strategy could give you a powerful competitive edge. 

Here are the three main benefits of marketing for real estate professionals: 

  • Builds trust with the customer base: A consistent presence assures potential buyers that they’re dealing with the right person to help them find their dream property. 
  • Makes the brand more memorable: A recognizable brand increases the chances that buyers will seek the brand out when they enter the market. 
  • Enables more efficient selling: A long-term marketing strategy provides established channels to quickly promote new properties when they become available, cutting down on promotion and admin costs. 

National Association of Realtors (NAR) data tells us that every buyer uses the internet at some point during their home search, and 46 percent take their first step online (versus 20 percent who start by contacting an agent). The marketing strategy used could be the difference between a brokerage that compounds visibility for years and one that keeps starting from zero on every new listing.

How to Build a Real Estate Marketing Plan

You can develop a solid real estate marketing management plan in five simple steps. The order matters because each step sets up the next, so don’t skip anything. It usually means going back to fix something later.

We’ll start with the most important step of any marketing plan: defining who you’re trying to reach. From there, we’ll discuss your brand’s presence and finish with the optimal digital strategy, as well as offline channels you can use to supplement it.

articles.title: How to find your social media target audience in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. A social media target audience is the specific group of people most likely to engage with your brand on social, defined by demographics, interests, behaviors, and stage in the customer journey.
  2. Your social media audience is not the same as your target market. Most brands need several audience segments across different platforms and campaigns.
  3. Analytics, social listening, and competitor analysis are the most reliable ways to identify and refine who you are actually reaching.
  4. Reaching your audience means matching platform, format, and message to each segment, then testing and adjusting based on performance data.

What is a social media target audience?

A social media target audience is a specific group of people your brand wants to reach on social media, based on shared traits like interests, behaviors, and demographics.

These are the users most likely to engage with your content, respond to your messaging, and convert into customers.

It is worth separating this from your general marketing audience. Someone might be a perfect customer for your product and still never see a single post, because they do not use the platforms you publish on or engage with the formats you produce. Your social media audience is defined as much by platform behavior as by buying potential.

For example, Momofuku Goods shares recipes modified for home cooks on their Instagram account. Of course, they incorporate Momofuku Goods products, but the recipes address a core interest of its audience.

Source: Momofukugoods

Understanding their target audience’s interest in cooking is a major contributing factor explaining why the Goods brand itself has over 182,000 followers.

In short: Your social media target audience is the slice of people you can realistically reach, and reliably engage, on the platforms where you publish.

Download now!

Social media target audience vs. target market: What is the difference?

A target market is the broad group of potential customers for your product or service, while a social media target audience is the narrower subset you aim to reach with a specific campaign or on a specific platform.

The target market is a business decision. The target audience is a channel decision. A running shoe brand might define its target market as recreational runners aged 25 to 55 in North America. On TikTok, its target audience might be first-time marathon trainees aged 22 to 30 who follow race-day content. Same company, much tighter group.

The simplest way to hold the difference: Your target market tells you who to sell to, and your social media target audience tells you who to talk to today.

Why does defining your social media target audience matter?

Defining your audience matters because it determines where your budget goes, what you publish, and whether any of it produces results you can measure.

Broad targeting feels safe, but it usually means diluted messaging, wasted paid spend, and content that no single group finds particularly relevant. A clearly defined audience gives you:

  • Focused messaging: You write for a specific person instead of a hypothetical average, which makes content sharper and easier to produce at scale.
  • Better return on spend: Narrow ad targeting reduces wasted impressions and improves the efficiency of every campaign dollar. It also makes your social media ROI easier to attribute.
  • Smarter platform selection: Knowing where your audience already spends time keeps teams from maintaining channels that never deliver.
  • Stronger brand relationships: Relevance compounds. People who consistently see content that matches their interests are far more likely to stick around.

For larger teams, there is a governance benefit too. When audience definitions are documented and shared as part of your broader social strategy, regional teams and agencies stay consistent instead of interpreting the brand differently on every channel.

What are the types of social media target audiences?

Social media target audiences are usually grouped by one of five approaches: demographics, psychographics, behavioral signals, purchase intent, or existing customer status. Most brands use a combination rather than picking just one.

Here are the main types of audience segmentation to work with:

  • Demographics
  • Psychographics
  • Behavioral signals
  • Purchase intent
  • Existing customers

Demographics

Demographics cover age, gender, level of education, location, and income level. They are the easiest data to pull and the easiest place to start, since every native analytics tool reports them.

One caveat worth repeating: Your social media target audience may not share the same demographics as your target audience for other marketing efforts. The people who buy from you and the people who follow you are often two overlapping but distinct groups.

You spent time crafting what you thought was a great meta description for your page. You agonized over word choice and character count for what felt like hours, only to have Google ignore it and choose a random sentence from your content to display as the search snippet. 

Why?

As social media users spread their attention across multiple platforms, more brands are expanding their presence to meet them there. According to our 2026 Social Media Content Strategy report, 87% of marketers plan to show up on more networks this year.

Cross-posting on social media is an excellent strategy for reaching new audiences, but it can also multiply your team’s workload, especially if you’re tailoring content to each platform.

This guide explains what cross-posting is, when it works (or backfires) and what each platform’s native rules allow. You’ll also learn how to cross-post easily with the Sprout Social Essentials plan.

What is cross-posting on social media?

Cross-posting means publishing the same content to two or more social media networks, either simultaneously or on a network-specific schedule.

But your posts shouldn’t be identical across platforms. A good cross-posting strategy preserves the core message or creative concept while optimizing the size, caption, format, tags, media and timing for each channel.

When you cross-post on social media effectively, you get content on your brand accounts quickly, freeing up your team for more strategic tasks like planning and engaging.

The right tools simplify the process. Sprout Social Essentials lets you cross-post to up to five social profiles at once. Use the unified Compose window to customize your post’s text, media and timing for each platform—no switching tabs.

Cross-posting vs. reposting vs. repurposing vs. sharing

Cross-posting, reposting, repurposing and sharing all extend the reach of your social content, but they describe different actions.

  • Cross-posting is when you publish your own content to several networks you control, with or without channel-specific editing.
  • Reposting is when you republish an existing post, yours or someone else’s, in its original form and usually within the same network.
  • Repurposing is when you rebuild an asset into one or several new formats to extend its life, increase reach and maximize ROI.
  • Sharing is when you distribute someone else’s post, either on your feed or to someone’s private inbox, through a native sharing button.

Here’s a quick table with examples of each term:

Term What it means Example Cross-posting Publishing one core post across multiple networks at the same time (or on an automated schedule) Publishing a ‘New Arrivals’ post on Instagram, LinkedIn and Facebook Reposting Resurfacing an existing post, yours or someone else’s, usually within the same network Reposting a customer’s Instagram post on your brand profile Repurposing Turning one asset into several different formats or deliverables Converting a webinar into three Reels and a LinkedIn carousel Sharing Distributing someone else’s post through a native sharing button Sharing a partner’s post to your feed or sending it through a direct message

Should you post the same content on every network?

Only cross-post content to networks where the topic is relevant and the format makes sense. Even then, “same content” should mean the same idea, not an untouched copy of the same post.

Exact duplication works for simple, time-sensitive updates. But for most campaigns, small changes to the hook, caption, tags, call-to-action, media and publish time give the post a better chance of meeting each audience’s expectations.

When cross-posting works well

Cross-posting works well when speed and consistency matter, or when audiences have similar needs across channels. Examples of content to cross-post include:

  • Company and product announcements: Launch dates, new locations, event registrations and important service updates benefit from a consistent message.
  • Evergreen education: Tips, how-to content, FAQs and research findings are useful across several networks, especially with minor tweaks.
  • Short-form video: A clean, watermark-free vertical video works across Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts.
  • Little to no audience overlap: If research shows your audience varies across platforms, cross-posting helps you reach more people without looking repetitive.

As for cadence, cross-post as often as the content fits each network, but balance it with platform-specific posts so every feed still feels original and worth following.

When to tailor or skip cross-posting

Create a separate post or stick to one network only when the content relies heavily on platform-specific behavior. Skip cross-posting in the following situations:

  • Format mismatch: A text-only update has no direct equivalent on TikTok, while a 10-minute landscape video won’t work on Instagram.
  • Overlapping audiences: Followers who see identical posts on several networks in quick succession will tune them out. Change the hook or stagger the timing.
  • Unique native features: Not every network supports features like polls, in-app sounds, stickers, live video, collaboration tools and document posts.
  • Varying audience expectations: Avoid cross-posting when content is built around platform-specific trends or needs a different angle, such as the business impact of an announcement on LinkedIn versus its human side on Instagram.

In these scenarios, the cons of cross-posting outweigh the pros. But that doesn’t mean cross-posting is bad for performance. Just avoid sharing identical or poorly adapted posts all the time as it makes your brand look repetitive and boring.

Benefits of cross-posting to multiple social channels

Cross-posting makes executing and scaling a multi-channel marketing strategy effortless. These five benefits show where cross-posting has the greatest impact.

Market to different target demographics

Cross-posting helps your brand reach different customer groups without recreating content from scratch every single time.

Every network has its own mix of age groups, interests, professions and behaviors. For example, the latest social media demographics show that Facebook reaches 88% of Baby Boomers, compared with 39% for Instagram and 20% for TikTok.

articles.fullContent:
Known and beloved for its compelling short-form video content, TikTok has become a social powerhouse in Australia. According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, 39% of Australian social users turn to TikTok to keep up with trends in many areas, from finance to fashion, technology to travel. For businesses, this level of engagement represents a major marketing opportunity—but only if they know exactly how and why Australians are using the app.

The latest TikTok statistics in Australia point to an app whose role keeps shifting. What started as an entertainment feed now shapes how Australians discover products, research big decisions and connect with the brands they love. Marketers who understand that shift meet their audience where attention already lives and turn casual scrolling into real business results.

In this guide, we cover the most important TikTok statistics in Australia to help you build a smarter, data-led strategy. With these insights, you can guide your social strategy, spark TikTok campaign ideas and create content that truly resonates with Australian audiences.

Key TikTok statistics in Australia

TikTok is a major player in Australia’s social media landscape. As of late 2025, 10.9 million Australians aged 18 and over use the app, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report. These statistics show how deeply the network has embedded itself into everyday life:

  • More than 350,000 Australian businesses use TikTok, restated by the company in 2026.

  • Australian users spend an average of 1 hour 14 minutes a day in the app (August 2025), the highest daily figure of any social app in Australia, per DataReportal and We Are Social.

  • Per a Deloitte report, Australian TikTok users spend most of their time on the app watching videos, listening to audio and browsing feeds.

  • According to Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report, short-form videos (<60 seconds long) perform best on TikTok. Users are most interested in entertaining content, product discovery and influencer partnerships

With Sprout Social, you can schedule TikTok posts, track performance and spot emerging trends from the same platform you use to manage every other network.

The rise of TikTok in Australia: TikTok stats on growth in the Australian market

Although it’s been a major player in Australia’s social media landscape for years, TikTok is constantly evolving. What primarily began as an entertainment platform has transformed into a source of information, an outlet for cultural connection and a driver for social change.

  • In Q4 2024 alone, TikTok generated 186 million downloads from users globally.

  • TikTok ads reached 51.2% of Australian adults aged 18 and over at the end of 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • TikTok’s ad reach grew 13.9% year-on-year in Australia, adding 1.33 million users, the fastest growth of any major Australian platform, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Australia counted 21.0 million social media user identities in October 2025, equal to 77.7% of the population, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to a 2024 report from Oxford Economics, 19% of Australian users have donated to a charity or cause they saw on TikTok, and 18% have committed their time to volunteer.

TikTok Australia user and demographic statistics

TikTok appeals strongly to younger audiences; over 30% of its global audience is aged 18–24. Given that young people are Australia’s most active social shoppers, TikTok is an ideal platform for brands to connect with and sell to these users. From gender to income, here’s a more in-depth look at Australian TikTokers:

  • Around 74% of TikTok’s Australian user base is younger than 34, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to Statista, around 53.1% of Australians aged 18 and over use TikTok.

  • 72% of Gen Z have TikTok accounts, compared with 50% of users overall, per Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report.

  • Almost half (48%) of Australians aged 18 to 24 use TikTok to get news, per the University of Canberra’s Digital News Report 2026.

  • According to Statista, TikTok is more popular with Gen Z than other social networks.

  • TikTok’s adult advertising audience in Australia was 53.6% male and 46.4% female in late 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Further, the 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report reveals that 37% of Millennials globally have TikTok accounts.

  • A 2024 survey found that 41% of Gen Z shoppers had made purchases through social media in the past six months, followed closely by Millennials (40%).

  • Statista reports that, while Millennials favour Facebook for social shopping, Instagram and TikTok attract more Zoomers.

Australia’s social media ban for children under 16 reshapes this picture. It removes under-16s from the platform, which shifts TikTok’s Australian audience even further towards adults. Here’s what that means for your strategy.

How does Australia’s under-16 social media ban affect TikTok?

Australia’s under-16 social media ban took effect on 10 December 2025 under the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2024. It requires TikTok and nine other social media platforms to take reasonable steps to stop Australians under 16 from holding accounts, with fines of up to A$49.5 million for non-compliance, per the eSafety Commissioner.

articles.title: Social media automation: A 3-step quick start guide for 2026

Between all the DMs you need to answer and the posts you need to create, it’s time-consuming to maintain an active social media presence. And as you expand to more channels without increasing headcount, you get sucked into a productivity trap where you’re doing more work, but your results stagnate.

This is all too familiar for social media teams that do (almost) everything manually. The Social Media Productivity Report from Sprout Social even found that 63% of are unable to do high-impact work because they’re bogged down by manual tasks.

On the other hand, respondents who use dedicated tools to manage their social media are twice as likely to have enough time to get their work done.

This makes a strong case for marketers to start automating various aspects of their social media management. In this social media automation guide, we break down three essential steps to get started. Let’s take a look.

What social media automation means

Social media automation is the process of letting tools handle routine and repetitive tasks like scheduling posts or tracking brand mentions. This gives you back the time needed for more meaningful work that requires human input, whether that’s responding to your DMs or creating high-quality content.

Rather than “replacing you,” automation allows you to free up time by automating the routine. So you have more time to spend on personalizing the meaningful.

Step 1: Centralize your publishing

Connect your profiles to one dashboard

You waste time when you’re manually logging into different profiles to schedule every post individually. Streamline the process by connecting all your social media profiles to a centralized publishing dashboard.

A social media management platform like Sprout consolidates your publishing through a single dashboard. This lets you connect your profiles across different social networks and manage your publishing in one place. When you create a new post to schedule, all you have to do is select the profile(s) where you want to publish it.

Build a lightweight content calendar

Before all the automation comes the planning. And you need to plan your posts ahead of time before you can schedule them.

A content calendar makes it easy to do this and organize your publishing efforts. When you already have content planned for the entire week or month, you can quickly start creating posts without spending too much time on ideation.

And you don’t have to build an elaborate calendar, either. Keep it simple with a clear outline of the essentials:

  • Platform and profile

But manually answering every message or question slows you down. While this keeps your brand human, it means people have to wait longer even for a generic question. That’s the part of engagement you can automate, giving you more time to focus on interactions that need a more tailored response.

Sprout’s Bot Builder lets you create chatbots and automate responses for frequently asked questions. This streamlines your X (Twitter) and Facebook automation efforts to speed up responses and field routine customer care enquiries.

articles.title: Reddit statistics in 2026 and tactics to grow your brand
articles.fullContent:
Reddit spent years as the internet’s best-kept secret. In 2026, the secret’s out. It’s one of the web’s fastest-growing platforms and a primary source powering AI search results. The conversations happening inside its communities shape what your customers read everywhere else.

That shift changes the math for marketers. Use these current Reddit statistics to benchmark your audience, understand user behavior and refine your Reddit marketing strategy.

Here’s what the latest data makes clear:

  • Reddit crossed 514.6 million weekly active uniques for the first time in Q2 2026, with daily active uniques up 18% year over year. Its audience is scaling fast, so early movers still have room to build authority.

  • The US is Reddit’s largest single market at 194.8 million users and 42.95% of traffic, but international daily users now outpace it. Your reach here isn’t capped by borders.

  • Only 22% of social users have a Reddit profile, yet the platform’s influence runs far deeper than that number suggests. Lurkers and searchers, not just registered accounts, drive its reach.

Reddit user demographics statistics

  • 48% of US adults who use Reddit are between 18–29 years old, followed by 30–49-year-olds.

  • As of 2026, 59.8% of users identified as male and 39.7% as female.

  • In 2025, US users’ ethnicities were 27% White, 18% Black, 22% Hispanic and 44% Asian.

  • Reddit’s largest audiences outside the US are in the UK (45.8 million), Canada (43.1 million), India (30.8 million), Germany (29.3 million) and Australia (23.3 million).

  • International daily users (77.1 million) now outpace US daily users (53.2 million) and are growing around 28% a year.

Reddit’s users lean young, making it a valuable social media platform for reaching Gen Z and younger millennials. While it reaches US audiences well, India, the United Kingdom and Canada also have notable bases.

These data points reveal a unique advantage for brands targeting social media demographics like Reddit’s through authenticity, community engagement and value-first organic interactions.

Targeting niche subreddits lets you focus on high-intent topics. Localized subreddits also allow teams to tailor campaigns by city or country.

Use these demographic insights to build a targeted Reddit marketing strategy that connects with high-intent audiences.

How Reddit users engage: Understanding behavior and traffic

On Reddit.com, you can increase engagement in a few ways. People spot your post or comment in their feed, or find you inside a specific subreddit. The other big driver is search engines.

Reddit is a popular place for real information. Because of Google’s $60 million yearly deal with Reddit and how people search, many internet users find Reddit posts through search engines.

Here are the key Reddit traffic and behavior numbers driving that discovery:

  • As of Q2 2026, Reddit reached over 130 million active daily users—77.7 million logged out and 52.6 million logged in.

  • That means 59.7% of daily users browse Reddit while logged out.

  • Organic search sends roughly 66.88% of Reddit’s traffic, which is exactly why that Google deal matters.

  • More than 80 million people search directly on Reddit each week.

  • Reddit has 2.3 billion backlinks from 1.4 million referring domains.

Foundation Marketing’s analysis of Reddit stats reveals key post performance benchmarks:

  • Titles between 160–180 characters earned the most upvotes.

  • The performance gap between question and non-question titles is now statistically negligible, under 1%.

  • Longer, descriptive titles consistently outperform very short ones.

Reddit user behavior & community norms

  • Redditors engage with authenticity: Reddit user behavior is often different from users on other social media platforms. They are invested in in-depth discussions about other people’s genuine thoughts, opinions and perspectives. Because of this, they’re invested in authentic discussions and are skeptical of promotional language and overt marketing.

  • All users are expected to respect subreddit rules and guidelines: Each subreddit has its own rules, guidelines and styles of engagement that all users are expected to follow. If you break those standards, you could easily lose trust, especially as a marketer. As a marketer, it’s important to understand community nuances and learn how users talk and think in the niche communities you’re involved in.

  • Users trust the authenticity of product reviews on Reddit: Since Reddit is a community-based platform, what users organically say about a product or business carries weight. To engage with redditors successfully, brands must join conversations and add enriching perspectives. And to maintain credibility across subreddits, avoid direct promotional pitches.

  • Redditors especially engage in the comments: The real value for users lies in the comment section of posts. Users have countless conversations that rabbit trail from the original post’s initial discussion. Your brand can hop into the myriad of conversations within just one thread and build relational equity within that community.
